The prior incident is anonymized and used solely for prevention and awareness. > > **Suggested footer on every slide:** > *Confidential — Internal Loss Prevention Use Only — Do Not Distribute Externally* --- ## Slide 1 — Title Slide # Missing Bank Deposits Investigation ### Incident Awareness and Investigation Guide **Supporting document for:** Loss Prevention Incident Flowchart **Audience:** Loss Prevention Investigators, Regional and District Leadership **Purpose:** Prevention, detection, investigation, and remediation of missing or delayed bank deposits --- ## Slide 2 — Incident Identification ### General Procedure Initiate review when any of the following occurs: - A deposit is not posted within the expected banking window. - Deposit timing differs from the store’s deposit log. - Bank-validated totals do not match store records. - Funds appear to leave the store and later reappear. - Deposits are repeatedly delayed, combined, or made out of sequence. - A deposit bag number, amount, preparer, courier, or bank receipt cannot be verified. - Cash overages or shortages fluctuate without a valid operational explanation. ### Prior Incident Awareness - A Store Manager had responsibility for taking cash deposits to the bank because the store did not use armored-car service. - Deposit records showed the cash as signed out from the store. - The deposits were not immediately placed in the bank’s deposit drop. - Funds were taken home and used for gambling. - After gambling winnings accumulated over several days, money was deposited later. - The delayed deposits caused unusual fluctuations and timing discrepancies in store funds. ### Prevention Lesson A deposit that eventually reaches the bank may still have been temporarily misappropriated. Investigators must evaluate **custody, timing, and unauthorized use**, not merely the ending bank balance. --- ## Slide 3 — Immediate Notification ### General Procedure Upon identifying a potentially missing or delayed deposit: 1. Notify the designated Loss Prevention leader. 2. Notify appropriate District or Regional management. 3. Engage Human Resources when employee misconduct may be involved. 4. Consult Legal Counsel based on loss amount, jurisdiction, evidence, or contemplated action. 5. Notify Treasury, Finance, or Cash Management so bank posting and account activity can be independently confirmed. 6. Restrict case communications to personnel with a business need to know. ### Prior Incident Awareness - Because a manager controlled the deposit process, the matter required independent escalation outside the store. - Store-level explanations alone could not be accepted without bank verification. - The position and authority of the person involved increased the need for confidentiality and objective oversight. ### Prevention Lesson When the suspected individual is a manager or controls relevant records, do not route the investigation exclusively through that person or permit that person to direct the response. --- ## Slide 4 — Protect Funds and Control Access ### General Procedure Immediately reduce additional exposure without compromising the investigation: - Count and secure remaining cash and prepared deposits. - Use two authorized employees to verify on-hand funds. - Reassign deposit preparation or transportation duties when authorized. - Secure deposit bags, bag inventory, safe keys, bank-drop keys, alarm codes, and deposit records. - Review access to cash offices, safes, deposit systems, and banking portals. - Preserve access logs before changing credentials. - Do not allow a suspected employee to remove documents or company property. - Coordinate any leave, suspension, or access restriction with HR and Legal. ### Prior Incident Awareness - One employee could sign deposits out and personally transport them. - The lack of armored-car service created direct custody risk. - There was insufficient independent verification that signed-out deposits actually reached the bank drop. ### Prevention Lesson Signing a deposit out of the store is not proof of bank delivery. The process must include independent, timely confirmation of receipt or posting. --- ## Slide 5 — Preserve Evidence ### General Procedure Preserve evidence before routine retention periods overwrite or destroy it. **Documents and records:** - Daily cash and sales reports - Deposit slips and bag numbers - Deposit preparation worksheets - Deposit sign-out and courier logs - Safe counts and opening/closing records - Bank receipts, images, posting reports, and adjustment notices - Employee schedules and time records - Key, alarm, and access-control logs - Relevant emails, texts, and business-system messages - Prior cash exception reports or audit findings **Video:** - Cash office and safe area - Store entrances and exits - Parking lot and employee vehicle area, where lawfully recorded - Deposit preparation and handoff points - Date and time synchronization information for each video system **Evidence controls:** - Preserve originals. - Work from copies where practical. - Record collector, date, time, source, and method. - Hash or otherwise authenticate exported electronic files when available. - Maintain a chain-of-custody log. ### Prior Incident Awareness Evidence needed to establish the gap between: - The time deposits were signed out, - The time the funds left the store, - The expected bank-drop time, and - The actual bank posting or deposit time. ### Prevention Lesson Delay in preservation may result in loss of video, access logs, or system records that establish custody and intent. --- ## Slide 6 — Preliminary Validation ### General Procedure Before concluding that theft occurred, independently validate: - The deposit amount expected by store records. - The date and time it was prepared. - The assigned transporter. - The deposit bag number and seal status. - The time it was signed out. - The expected banking cutoff and posting window. - Weekends, holidays, bank outages, or processing delays. - Whether the bank has an unposted or misapplied deposit. - Whether the deposit was posted under the wrong date, store, account, or amount. - Whether a clerical error explains the discrepancy. ### Prior Incident Awareness - The fluctuation initially could have appeared to be a timing or reconciliation problem. - The material issue was that deposits were delayed for several days after leaving company custody. - Subsequent deposits did not validate proper handling of the original funds. ### Prevention Lesson Separate legitimate bank processing delays from an unexplained gap in physical custody. --- ## Slide 7 — Explained by Verified Bank or Clerical Error? ### Decision Standard A case may be treated as a verified processing or clerical exception only when objective evidence establishes: - The funds remained under authorized control. - No employee used or diverted the funds. - The deposit delay was caused by a documented bank or administrative issue. - The complete amount is traceable from store records to the bank. - All dates, amounts, bag numbers, and custodians reconcile. ### If “Yes” - Document the explanation. - Attach bank or system verification. - Correct the reconciliation. - Identify and remediate the process weakness. - Continue monitoring for recurrence. ### If “No” - Open a formal investigation. - Do not accept unsupported verbal explanations. - Preserve all evidence and establish a full chronology. ### Prior Incident Awareness The later appearance of money in the bank did not establish a clerical error. The deposits had been removed, personally used, and replaced or deposited later. --- ## Slide 8 — Document and Correct ### General Procedure For a verified non-theft discrepancy: - Record the issue, root cause, affected amount, and dates. - Identify who discovered and resolved it. - Attach independent bank confirmation. - Correct accounting entries. - Retrain responsible employees. - Modify controls to prevent recurrence. - Set a follow-up review date. - Escalate repeated “clerical” discrepancies for trend analysis. ### Prior Incident Awareness The incident demonstrates why repeated delayed deposits should not be normalized as harmless timing issues. ### Prevention Lesson A recurring deposit delay can be a behavioral indicator, especially when one employee controls preparation, sign-out, transport, and reconciliation. --- ## Slide 9 — Open Formal Investigation ### General Procedure The assigned investigator should create a written case plan that includes: - Allegation and source - Known and potentially affected deposit dates - Estimated financial exposure - Relevant employees and witnesses - Systems and records to be examined - Evidence-preservation actions - Interview order - Required approvals - Legal, privacy, labor, and safety considerations - Target completion dates ### Scope Guidance Review enough history to identify whether the event was: - Isolated, - Repeated, - Escalating, - Concealed through later deposits, - Associated with other shortages, or - Enabled by a broader control failure. ### Prior Incident Awareness The review needed to extend beyond one missing deposit because delayed deposits over several days could create a rolling concealment pattern. --- ## Slide 10 — Records and Transaction Review ### General Procedure Trace each deposit through the complete chain: 1. Sales and cash generation 2. Register or cash-office reconciliation 3. Deposit preparation 4. Bag sealing and recording 5. Safe storage 6. Sign-out and transfer of custody 7. Removal from the store 8. Delivery to the bank drop 9. Bank receipt or image 10. Account posting and reconciliation ### Analytical Tests - Compare sign-out time with actual posting time. - Identify deposits made out of sequence. - Compare amounts for evidence of substitution or rolling repayment. - Review deposits clustered after unusual delays. - Look for amounts split or combined without authorization. - Compare duties, schedules, and access. - Examine prior exceptions involving the same custodian. - Determine whether later funds may have been used to cover earlier shortages. ### Prior Incident Awareness The manager signed out deposits, retained them outside authorized custody, gambled with the funds, and deposited money several days later. The sequence created balance fluctuations that could conceal temporary use. ### Prevention Lesson Focus on whether the **same physical funds** were delivered as required and whether company money was continuously safeguarded. --- ## Slide 11 — Video and Access Review ### General Procedure Use video and access data to corroborate, not replace, financial records. Review: - Deposit preparation and sealing - Safe access - Deposit removal - Employee entry and exit - Whether the assigned employee left with the deposit - Whether another person received or handled it - Return visits inconsistent with records - Access outside normal schedules - Discrepancies between recorded and actual activity ### Documentation - Record camera name, location, and system time. - Note any difference between video time and actual time. - Preserve relevant periods before and after the event. - Capture both inculpatory and exculpatory evidence. - Avoid conclusions that exceed what the video shows. ### Prior Incident Awareness Video and access records could help establish when the deposits left the store and whether the custodian’s actions matched the written deposit log. --- ## Slide 12 — Subject and Witness Interviews ### General Procedure Conduct interviews lawfully, fairly, and without coercion. **Before the interview:** - Review the evidence and identify gaps. - Determine interview order. - Coordinate with HR or Legal as required. - Select a private, professional setting. - Confirm any representation rights. - Use two company representatives when appropriate. **During the interview:** - Explain the general purpose without making premature accusations. - Ask open-ended questions first. - Obtain the employee’s description of normal deposit procedures. - Establish dates, times, amounts, custody, route, and bank-drop practices. - Present evidence progressively. - Seek clarification of contradictions. - Ask about missing records, delays, and the location of funds. - Allow the employee to provide exculpatory information. - Document responses accurately. **Prohibited or high-risk practices:** - Threats, intimidation, promises, or coercion - Unlawful detention or search - Misrepresenting legal authority - Demanding repayment as a condition of release - Secret recording without legal authorization - Discriminatory or retaliatory conduct ### Prior Incident Awareness Relevant subjects included the deposit custodian and employees who prepared, witnessed, reconciled, or questioned the deposits. The interview should address why signed-out funds were not immediately delivered and how later deposits were funded. --- ## Slide 13 — Findings and Escalation ### General Procedure Evaluate the evidence against company policy and applicable law. Potential findings include: - Procedural noncompliance - Negligent handling - Falsification of records - Unauthorized retention of funds - Temporary misappropriation - Theft or embezzlement - Concealment through delayed or replacement deposits - Supervisory or control failures - Unsubstantiated allegation ### Escalation Factors - Amount and duration of exposure - Repetition or pattern - Position of trust - Falsified records - Attempted concealment - Admission or corroborating evidence - Impact on financial reporting - Risk to customers or other employees - Insurance, bonding, or law-enforcement requirements - Regulatory or contractual obligations ### Prior Incident Awareness Even though funds were deposited later, taking company cash home and gambling with it represented unauthorized personal use and a serious breach of trust and deposit policy. --- ## Slide 14 — Evidence Supports Misconduct or Theft? ### Decision Standard A substantiated finding should be based on the totality of reliable evidence, which may include: - Documentary records - Bank data - Video - Access logs - Witness statements - Subject statements or admissions - Reconciliation analysis - Pattern evidence - Evidence of unauthorized possession or use ### Important Principle The return, replacement, or later deposit of company funds does not automatically negate: - Unauthorized control, - Deprivation of company access, - Falsification, - Misuse, - Policy violations, or - Potential criminal exposure. ### Required Review Before final action, obtain required approval from: - Loss Prevention leadership - Human Resources - Legal Counsel - Relevant business leadership --- ## Slide 15 — Case Closure: Unsubstantiated ### General Procedure If available evidence does not substantiate misconduct: - Document what was alleged. - Summarize all investigative steps. - Identify evidence reviewed. - Explain why the allegation was not substantiated. - Preserve records according to retention requirements. - Avoid labeling an employee as culpable without sufficient evidence. - Correct any control weakness discovered. - Monitor relevant deposit activity for a defined period. - Reopen the case if material new evidence emerges. ### Prior Incident Awareness An eventual deposit should not automatically produce an “unsubstantiated” result. Closure must address the entire custody gap and verify that no unauthorized use occurred. --- ## Slide 16 — Management, HR, and Legal Action ### General Procedure When evidence supports misconduct: - Present an objective case summary. - Separate facts, admissions, inferences, and unresolved issues. - Follow the company’s disciplinary approval process. - Apply policy consistently. - Coordinate timing of access removal, property recovery, and employment action. - Determine whether law enforcement should be contacted. - Determine whether insurer, bonding company, auditor, or banking partner notice is required. - Preserve evidence regardless of whether employment action is taken. ### Law-Enforcement Considerations Company leadership and Legal Counsel should assess: - Strength and admissibility of evidence - Loss amount and duration - Jurisdiction - Employee admissions - Recovery status - Insurance requirements - Safety and business-continuity concerns ### Prior Incident Awareness The employee’s management position and misuse of entrusted deposits required escalation beyond routine performance management. --- ## Slide 17 — Recovery and Reconciliation ### General Procedure Recovery efforts must be lawful and separately documented from the fact-finding process. - Confirm every affected deposit and amount. - Distinguish original funds from later replacement funds when possible. - Reconcile store and bank records. - Document restitution, recovered property, or bank adjustments. - Issue receipts for any authorized repayment. - Do not promise that repayment will prevent discipline or prosecution. - Do not pressure an employee into unauthorized wage deductions. - Preserve evidence even after full recovery. - Coordinate accounting treatment with Finance. ### Prior Incident Awareness The later deposit of money reduced or eliminated an apparent cash shortage at a point in time, but it did not erase the prior unauthorized use or custody violation. --- ## Slide 18 — Corrective Action and Prevention ### Required Control Improvements **Deposit preparation and custody** - Separate deposit preparation, verification, transport, and reconciliation where staffing permits. - Require two-person verification of deposit amount, bag number, and seal. - Prohibit one person from controlling the entire process. - Keep prepared deposits in a secured safe until transfer. - Maintain controlled inventories of deposit bags and keys. **Transportation** - Use armored-car service where risk, volume, or geography supports it. - If employee transport is necessary, use a written authorized-courier process. - Establish delivery deadlines and escalation rules. - Prohibit taking deposits home or making personal stops. - Avoid publicizing routes, times, or cash amounts. - Address employee safety; employees should not pursue robbers or resist a robbery. **Independent confirmation** - Require bank receipt, validated drop record, or electronic posting confirmation. - Compare deposits signed out with bank activity daily. - Escalate any unposted deposit immediately after the approved window. - Assign reconciliation to someone independent of the courier. - Require documented supervisor review. **Monitoring** - Report delayed, out-of-sequence, split, combined, or fluctuating deposits. - Analyze trends by store, custodian, day, and amount. - Perform unannounced audits. - Rotate duties and require vacations where appropriate. - Review manager overrides and recurring reconciliation adjustments. ### Prior Incident Awareness The principal control failure was the ability of a single manager to sign out deposits, retain physical custody, delay delivery, and benefit personally before later depositing funds. --- ## Slide 19 — Final Report and Awareness Brief ### Final Report Structure 1. Executive summary 2. Allegation and discovery method 3. Scope and methodology 4. Chronology 5. Deposit-by-deposit reconciliation 6. Evidence reviewed 7. Interviews conducted 8. Established facts 9. Subject explanations 10. Findings and policy implications 11. Financial exposure and recovery 12. Management, HR, Legal, and law-enforcement actions 13. Root cause and control failures 14. Corrective-action owner and due date 15. Follow-up testing plan ### Anonymized Awareness Brief - Do not include names, store number, personal identifiers, or unnecessary geographic detail. - Describe the method, indicators, control failures, and prevention measures. - Avoid speculation about addiction, motive, or medical condition. - State only facts supported by the investigation. - Distribute only to authorized Loss Prevention and business leaders. ### Prior Incident Summary for Internal Awareness An employee entrusted with transporting bank deposits signed cash deposits out of a store that did not use armored-car service. Instead of immediately placing the bags in the bank’s deposit drop, the employee took the funds home and gambled with them. After accumulating gambling winnings over several days, funds were deposited later, causing fluctuations and timing discrepancies. The incident demonstrates that eventual bank posting does not prove continuous safeguarding or proper custody. --- ## Slide 20 — Regional and District Awareness Actions ### Loss Prevention Investigator Checklist - Review every store that uses employee-transported deposits. - Identify stores where a manager performs preparation, transport, and reconciliation. - Confirm each store has a documented deposit-delivery deadline. - Verify how bank receipt or posting is independently confirmed. - Test a sample of signed-out deposits against bank records. - Review delayed and out-of-sequence deposits for at least the locally approved lookback period. - Confirm video-retention periods cover the normal reconciliation cycle. - Ensure deposit-bag and key controls are documented. - Train District and Store Managers on immediate escalation. - Report material gaps and remediation dates to Regional Loss Prevention leadership. ### Key Awareness Message > **A deposit is not complete when it leaves the store. It is complete only when authorized delivery is independently verified and the funds are reconciled to the bank.** --- ## Slide 21 — Warning Indicators ### Deposit-Related Red Flags - Repeated explanations that the bank “posted late” - Missing bank receipts - Handwritten or altered deposit logs - Deposits posted several days after sign-out - Multiple deposits posted together - Deposits posted out of sequence - Recurring shortages followed by unexplained corrections - One person insisting on exclusive control of deposits - Unusual resistance to armored service, dual control, or independent reconciliation - Personal stops or unexplained route deviations during deposit transport - Frequent deposit-bag replacements or inconsistent bag numbers - Manager overrides that close reconciliation exceptions - Fluctuating balances that resolve shortly before audits or reporting deadlines ### Caution Red flags justify review; they do not independently prove theft. --- ## Slide 22 — Management Discussion Questions 1. Which locations still use employee transportation for cash deposits? 2. Who can prepare, sign out, transport, and reconcile deposits? 3. How quickly is a missed posting identified? 4. Who receives the exception alert? 5. Can the transporter explain away the exception without independent bank verification? 6. Are weekends, holidays, and banking cutoffs formally addressed? 7. Are employees ever permitted to take deposits home? **Required answer: No.** 8. Is there evidence that every signed-out bag reached the bank? 9. Are delayed deposits reviewed for patterns rather than in isolation? 10. Have corrective controls been tested after implementation? --- ## Slide 23 — Closing # Protect the Chain of Custody - Verify the deposit before it leaves. - Control who may transport it. - Confirm delivery independently. - Investigate every unexplained delay. - Preserve evidence promptly. - Apply policy consistently. - Share anonymized lessons to prevent recurrence. **Confidential — Internal Loss Prevention Use Only**

### Rating Instructions

Mark one response for every checklist item:

- **Y — Compliant:** Requirement is fully met.
- **N — Missed Item:** Requirement is not met, is only partially met, or cannot be verified.
- **N/A — Not Applicable:** Requirement does not apply to this store. Explain in the comments.
- **Critical:** A condition that presents an imminent threat, affects emergency systems or egress, involves serious food-safety risk, or represents a potentially serious regulatory violation.

**Verification methods:**  
**O** = Observation · **R** = Record review · **I** = Employee interview

### Immediate Escalation Rule

The monthly score does **not** replace immediate action. Any imminent hazard must be isolated or corrected at once. Examples include:

- Blocked or locked emergency exits;
- Fire protection equipment out of service;
- Exposed energized electrical components;
- Active gas, refrigerant, chemical, or significant water leak;
- Unsafe structural condition;
- Suspected foodborne illness event or uncontrolled temperature abuse;
- Missing required emergency response capability;
- Any condition presenting an immediate risk of serious injury.

Notify the Manager on Duty and follow company emergency/escalation procedures. Contact emergency services or the appropriate authority when required.

# 3. Scoring and Compliance Determination

## Scoring Rules

1. Count every **No** response as one missed item.
2. Exclude properly justified **N/A** responses from applicable items.
3. **Applicable Items = Yes + No**
4. **Compliance Percentage = Yes ÷ Applicable Items × 100**
5. The checklist contains **124 total items** before N/A exclusions.
6. A store may miss **up to 10 items** without triggering the mandatory District Manager corrective action plan.
7. **More than 10 missed items requires a detailed corrective action plan submitted to the District Manager.**
8. Every missed item must still be corrected and tracked, even when the store has 10 or fewer misses.
9. Any critical deficiency requires immediate control and escalation, regardless of total score.

# Proposal for Local Assembly of EV Battery Packs in India  
**To:** Chief Procurement Officer  
**From:** Senior Manager—EV Battery Sourcing  
**Subject:** EvTronics–EV Batteries Inc. Partnership for Battery Pack Assembly Localisation  
**Date:** 24 March 2026  
**Decision required:** Approval to initiate commercial and technical due diligence and negotiate a five-year localisation agreement

---

## 1. Executive Summary

To support the company’s three recently launched electric vehicle models and progressively meet India’s localisation objectives, we propose establishing a local battery-pack assembly operation in Delhi through a partnership between:

- **EvTronics: 49% ownership**, leading local assembly and operations; and  
- **EV Batteries Inc.: 51% ownership**, retaining technical oversight, product/process control, and responsibility for child-part supply.

EV Batteries Inc. would continue supplying battery cells, housing, thermal systems, battery management system (BMS), and connectors. These parts would be imported into India and assembled by the partnership into complete battery packs for delivery to our plant.

The proposal initially localises **assembly and associated overhead only**; component pricing is assumed unchanged. At an expected volume of **110,000 packs per year for five years**, local assembly reduces the pack cost from **₹830,000 to ₹722,690**, generating a saving of:

- **₹107,310 per battery pack**
- **₹1,180.41 crore annually**
- **₹5,902.05 crore over five years**, before capex, financing, taxes, duties, logistics changes, and transition costs

The model supports early-stage localisation and builds a platform for subsequent localisation of the housing, connectors, thermal systems, BMS, and ultimately cells and advanced electronics. Approval is recommended subject to validation of regulatory eligibility, landed component costs, capex, quality readiness, and enforceable technology-transfer commitments.

---

## 2. Strategic Context and Partnership Structure

### 2.1 Rationale

The current arrangement—importing fully assembled packs from EV Batteries Inc.—limits domestic value addition and exposes the company to foreign-exchange volatility, international logistics disruption, and potential loss of localisation-linked incentives. At the same time, projected demand does not support a standalone Indian facility for EV Batteries Inc.

A jointly governed operation combines EV Batteries Inc.’s battery technology and manufacturing expertise with EvTronics’ local footprint, labour access, supplier network, and electronics-assembly capability. The committed five-year volume of **550,000 packs** materially improves utilisation and investment viability.

> **Regulatory note:** The stated FAME II/PMP phase structure has been used as the planning framework provided for this proposal. Before investment, Legal and Government Affairs must confirm the incentives and localisation rules applicable to the company’s vehicle category and production period, including any successor schemes.

### 2.2 Proposed Operating Structure

| Area | EvTronics—49% | EV Batteries Inc.—51% | Our Company |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary role | Delhi operations and local assembly | Technical oversight and controlling interest | Anchor customer and programme governance |
| Manufacturing | Labour, line operation, maintenance, warehousing | Process design, tooling specifications, validation | Audit rights and production approval |
| Supply chain | Local logistics and future local suppliers | Imported child parts and supplier quality | Forecasts and localisation targets |
| Quality | In-process and end-of-line execution | Product standards, traceability, engineering changes | Incoming quality and warranty monitoring |
| Technology | Workforce deployment and capability building | Training, documentation, software and know-how | Approve technology-transfer milestones |
| Commercial | Local operating-cost control | Child-part pricing and supply continuity | Volume commitment subject to performance |

A shareholders’ agreement should reserve critical decisions—technology changes, sourcing changes, related-party pricing, capacity expansion, and quality release—for joint approval, despite EV Batteries Inc.’s 51% ownership.

---

## 3. Sourcing Model and Financial Assessment

### 3.1 Proposed Material Flow

1. EV Batteries Inc. supplies validated cells, housing, thermal systems, BMS, and connectors.
2. Parts are imported into the Delhi operation using agreed Incoterms and inventory norms.
3. EvTronics leads module/pack assembly, software flashing, sealing, end-of-line testing, traceability, and dispatch.
4. Completed packs are supplied locally to our vehicle plant under an agreed quality, delivery, warranty, and cost framework.
5. Future sourcing waves shift selected child parts to approved Indian suppliers.

### 3.2 Cost-Saving Calculation

**Exchange rate:** USD 1 = ₹83  
**Annual volume:** 110,000 packs  
**Analysis period:** Five years  
**Total volume:** 550,000 packs

| Cost element per pack | Current imported pack | Locally assembled pack | Saving |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Components other than assembly/overhead | ₹705,500 | ₹705,500 | — |
| Assembly | ₹107,900 | ₹20,000 | ₹87,900 |
| Overhead | ₹16,600 | ₹590 | ₹16,010 |
| **Total pack cost** | **₹830,000** | **₹726,090** | **₹103,910** |

**Calculation basis**

- Current assembly: USD 1,300 × ₹83 = **₹107,900**
- Current overhead: USD 200 × ₹83 = **₹16,600**
- Unchanged components: ₹830,000 − ₹107,900 − ₹16,600 = **₹705,500**
- Local pack cost: ₹705,500 + ₹20,000 + ₹590 = **₹726,090**
- Saving per pack: ₹830,000 − ₹726,090 = **₹103,910**

### 3.3 Volume and Gross Savings Outlook

| Year | Expected packs | Gross saving per pack | Annual gross saving |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Year 1 | 110,000 | ₹103,910 | ₹1,143.01 crore |
| Year 2 | 110,000 | ₹103,910 | ₹1,143.01 crore |
| Year 3 | 110,000 | ₹103,910 | ₹1,143.01 crore |
| Year 4 | 110,000 | ₹103,910 | ₹1,143.01 crore |
| Year 5 | 110,000 | ₹103,910 | ₹1,143.01 crore |
| **Five-year total** | **550,000** | — | **₹5,715.05 crore** |

This represents a **12.5% gross reduction** versus the current pack price. The saving is significant, but it is not yet a full business-case net benefit.

### 3.4 Important Assumptions and Sensitivities

The estimate assumes all non-assembly component costs remain unchanged. Final economics must additionally account for:

- Partnership capex, depreciation, financing, and ramp-up losses
- Import duties and freight for child parts versus complete packs
- Packaging, local logistics, inventory carrying cost, insurance, and taxes
- Scrap, yield loss, utilities, testing consumables, warranty, and rework
- Transfer pricing and any technical licence or royalty fees
- Exchange-rate movement on the **₹705,500 imported content per pack**
- Incentives or tax benefits confirmed as legally available

Assembly localisation reduces forex exposure by approximately **₹124,500 per pack** of current foreign-denominated assembly and overhead content. However, most pack value remains import-linked until components are localised.

---

## 4. Phased Localisation Roadmap

| Timing | Localisation scope | Principal actions and decision gates |
|---|---|---|
| **0–6 months: Establish** | Partnership and plant planning | Shareholders’ agreement; detailed business case; Delhi site selection; capex approval; licences; equipment ordering; supply and technology-transfer contracts |
| **6–12 months: Industrialise** | Pilot local pack assembly | Install line; train operators; establish traceability and safety systems; pilot builds; PPAP/validation; controlled start of production |
| **Years 1–2: Phase 1** | Full local pack assembly | Ramp to 110,000 packs/year; stabilise quality, yield, and delivery; qualify local packaging and consumables |
| **Years 3–5: Phase 2** | Selected mechanical/electrical parts | Localise housing, brackets, busbars, harnesses, connectors, cooling plates/thermal hardware where commercially and technically viable |
| **Years 5–9: Phase 3** | BMS and deeper power-electronics content | Local PCB assembly, BMS hardware, thermal controllers and software capability; strengthen domestic validation and engineering-change capability |
| **Year 9 onward: Phase 4** | Cells, semiconductors, advanced electronics | Evaluate domestic cell offtake/JV opportunities and locally sourced semiconductor/electronic assemblies, subject to scale and technology maturity |

Each wave should proceed only after meeting cost, safety, reliability, capacity, and regulatory thresholds. Dual sourcing should be retained for high-risk components where feasible.

---

## 5. Benefits, Risks, and Mitigations

### Key Benefits

- **Localisation alignment:** Establishes domestic battery-pack assembly and a credible path toward deeper domestic value addition.
- **Material cost reduction:** Potential gross saving of **₹5,715.05 crore over five years** before incremental costs.
- **Lower forex exposure:** Eliminates imported assembly and overhead content, with further reduction as child parts localise.
- **Supply-chain resilience:** Shorter finished-pack lead time, faster issue resolution, and lower dependence on international movement of complete packs.
- **Capability creation:** Builds local battery manufacturing, testing, traceability, and supplier-development skills.
- **Scalable investment model:** Shared facility economics address EV Batteries Inc.’s concern regarding standalone investment viability.

### Principal Risks and Required Mitigations

| Risk | Impact | Proposed mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Continued dependence on imported cells and electronics | Forex, geopolitical, customs, and supply disruption | Safety stock; multi-route logistics; cell allocation commitment; business-continuity plan; future second-source qualification |
| Partnership and coordination complexity | Slow decisions and unclear accountability | Reserved matters, RACI, joint steering committee, escalation timelines, open-book costing |
| Initial capex and volume underutilisation | Longer payback and higher unit cost | Modular line, milestone-based investment, flexible capacity, volume bands, capex contribution negotiation |
| Quality or safety issues during ramp-up | Vehicle launch disruption, recall, reputational damage | EV Batteries Inc. resident engineering team, PPAP, pilot builds, end-of-line testing, layered audits, warranty allocation |
| Technology-transfer limitations | Long-term dependency on foreign partner | Contracted transfer milestones, training hours, documentation access, software/interface rights, local engineering targets |
| Regulatory interpretation risk | Incentive loss despite investment | Obtain written legal/tax assessment and, where possible, clarification from the relevant authority before commitment |
| Related-party child-part pricing | Erosion of projected savings | Benchmarking, price-index formula, audit rights, annual productivity targets, most-favoured pricing protection |

---

## 6. Recommendation and Next Steps

Proceed with the EvTronics–EV Batteries Inc. partnership to the due-diligence and negotiation stage. The strategic logic is strong and the preliminary gross saving is substantial, but final approval should be conditional on a complete landed-cost and investment case.

### Actions for the Next 90 Days

1. **Approve a joint feasibility team** across Procurement, Engineering, Manufacturing, Finance, Tax, Legal, Quality, and Government Affairs.
2. **Validate regulatory qualification** of local assembly and establish the domestic-value calculation methodology.
3. **Issue a detailed RFQ/business-case template** covering child-part prices, duties, logistics, capex, royalties, labour, utilities, scrap, warranty, and working capital.
4. **Conduct EvTronics capability and Delhi-site audits**, including battery safety, fire protection, hazardous-material handling, traceability, and workforce readiness.
5. **Negotiate binding commercial protections:** five-year pricing, productivity glide path, open-book costing, audit rights, capacity reservation, service levels, warranty allocation, and business continuity.
6. **Define technology-transfer deliverables** and measurable localisation gates for housing, connectors, thermal systems, BMS, and other parts.
7. **Run pilot validation and PPAP** before transferring series volume; retain imported finished packs as temporary launch contingency.
8. **Return for final investment approval** with net savings, capex, NPV, payback period, incentive confirmation, and downside scenarios.

**Recommended CPO decision:** Authorise commercial negotiations and technical due diligence, with final award contingent upon regulatory confirmation, validated net economics, successful pilot qualification, and an enforceable technology-transfer and localisation roadmap.

## 1. Objective and Guiding Principles

The proposed workflow replaces hard-copy approval files and repeated full-cycle negotiations with a digitally governed, configuration-based sourcing process. It is designed to accommodate frequent lamp design changes—such as variant additions, styling revisions, technology upgrades, and child-part changes—without compromising cost control, quality, traceability, or program timelines.

### Target Outcomes

- Reduce sourcing delays caused by post-nomination changes, with a target of **at least 30% reduction in change approval lead time**.
- Create one digital source of truth for TRSOs, supplier evaluations, quotations, negotiations, approvals, nominations, and subsequent changes.
- Enable **plug-and-play commercial evaluation** through modular quotation structures.
- Avoid reopening the entire sourcing process when a change remains within pre-approved technical, commercial, and capacity boundaries.
- Provide real-time visibility of ownership, status, aging, risks, and impact on program milestones.
- Retain complete, time-stamped evidence of decisions, communications, and approvals.

### Governing Principles

1. **Configuration rather than document-based sourcing:** Each lamp is managed as a baseline configuration plus selectable modules.
2. **One change, one impact assessment:** Technical, cost, quality, capacity, tooling, and timing impacts are assessed in parallel.
3. **Approval by exception:** Pre-agreed changes follow a fast track; only material deviations require full reapproval or resourcing.
4. **No approval by silence:** Every approval must be explicit, attributable, and time-stamped.
5. **Immutable audit trail:** Approved records are version-controlled and cannot be overwritten.
6. **Segregation of duties:** Requesting, evaluating, approving, and releasing commercial decisions remain role-separated.

---

## 2. Modular Quotation Structure

Each supplier quotation shall use a standardized digital cost model maintained at lamp-family and variant level. The nominated baseline will be locked, while individual modules may be added, removed, or changed without rebuilding the complete quotation.

### 2.1 Mandatory Quotation Modules

| Cost module | Required breakdown and examples |
|---|---|
| **Base assembly** | Housing, lens, bezel, reflector, standard seals, fasteners, assembly labor, testing and packing |
| **Feature modules** | LED/halogen source, DRL, sequential indicator, adaptive lighting, leveling, animation, diagnostics, communication protocol |
| **Design/aesthetic modules** | Styling insert, lens texture or color, light guide, reflector finish, decorative coating, signature graphic |
| **Child-part modules** | LED PCB, driver, control unit, connector, harness, motor/actuator, sensor, fan, heat sink, gasket |
| **Raw-material modules** | Polycarbonate, polypropylene, ABS, aluminum, copper, electronics/semiconductors, coating and adhesive |
| **Manufacturing/process modules** | Molding, metallization, coating, welding, potting, assembly, end-of-line testing, special inspection |
| **Tooling and development** | Tool-wise investment, modification cost, gauges, fixtures, validation, software/NRE and amortization basis |
| **Commercial/logistics** | Conversion cost, overhead, profit, freight, packaging, duties/taxes, warranty provision and payment terms |
| **Localization module** | Current and proposed source, local content percentage, localization timeline, investment, savings and dependency risk |
| **Economic adjustment** | Indexed material content, agreed benchmark/index, base month, foreign-exchange exposure, reset frequency and formula |

### 2.2 Required Commercial Logic

For every module, suppliers shall provide:

- Part/module identifier linked to TRSO and BOM;
- Quantity or usage per lamp and applicable variants;
- Unit cost, tooling/NRE, capacity and lead time;
- Technical assumptions, exclusions, validity, and minimum economic volume;
- “Add,” “delete,” and “replace” prices;
- Cost-driver formula, including material weight, index sensitivity, exchange-rate sensitivity, and volume band;
- Effective date and evidence supporting requested revisions.

The platform will calculate the price of a selected configuration as:

> **Configuration Price = Base Assembly + Selected Feature/Design/Child-Part Modules ± Raw-Material and FX Adjustments + Logistics/Commercial Elements**

Approved modules constitute a **commercial envelope**. A post-nomination change that uses an approved module and remains within agreed thresholds can be processed without renegotiating unaffected elements.

---

## 3. End-to-End Digital Workflow and Decision Gates

### Step 1 — Digital Sourcing Request and TRSO Baseline

ER initiates the sourcing request and uploads the structured TRSO, drawings, styling data, performance targets, interfaces, validation requirements, forecast volumes, variants, regulatory requirements, and target milestones. Program Management confirms program scope and timing.

**Gate G0 – Request Readiness**

- **Approvers:** ER, Quality, Purchase and Program Manager  
- **Checks:** TRSO completeness; requirement maturity; variant strategy; target dates; preliminary risk classification  
- **Output:** Version-controlled baseline and unique sourcing case ID  
- **Rule:** Incomplete requirements are returned with owner and due date; no RFQ is issued without G0 approval.

### Step 2 — Supplier Discovery, Screening and Longlisting

Purchase creates the longlist using approved supplier records and market intelligence. Suppliers are screened for technical competency, lamp technology, design capability, manufacturing footprint, capacity, financial health, reliability, quality systems, localization potential, cybersecurity/IP controls, and past performance.

**Gate G1 – RFQ Bidder Approval**

- **Approvers:** Purchase and Quality; ER concurrence for technical capability  
- **Output:** Approved bidder list, supplier risks, and mitigation actions  
- **Escalation:** High-risk or single-source strategy requires CPO/delegated authority approval.

### Step 3 — Structured RFQ and Modular Quotations

Purchase releases a common digital RFQ package containing the TRSO baseline, configurable variant matrix, modular quotation template, demand bands, localization expectations, nomination conditions, and milestone plan. Supplier questions and responses are maintained within the case record and made visible to all relevant evaluators.

The platform validates completeness, flags inconsistent assumptions, normalizes currency and economic factors, and creates like-for-like cost comparisons.

### Step 4 — Parallel Technical, Quality, Capacity and Commercial Evaluation

Functions assess bids concurrently:

- **ER:** design solution, performance, interfaces, technology roadmap, validation effort and design-change resilience;
- **Quality:** QMS maturity, process capability, warranty risk, traceability, testing and audit results;
- **Purchase:** landed cost, cost breakdown, module pricing, competitiveness, capacity, localization and negotiation strategy;
- **Finance:** business case, tooling/NRE, indexation, exchange exposure and affordability;
- **Program Manager:** milestone feasibility, variant coverage and program risk.

A weighted scorecard and unresolved deviation log are generated automatically.

**Gate G2 – Shortlist and Negotiation Mandate**

- **Approvers:** Purchase, ER, Quality and Program Manager; Finance validates commercial baseline  
- **Output:** Shortlist, negotiation targets, walk-away positions and open-risk register.

### Step 5 — Negotiation and Commercial Envelope Agreement

Negotiations shall cover both the baseline lamp and future flexibility. The record will capture meeting minutes, supplier responses, revised quote versions, should-cost gaps, concessions, indexation formulae, tooling ownership, capacity reservation, localization commitments, warranty, change lead times, and module add/delete rules.

No offline commitment is valid unless recorded and acknowledged in the platform.

**Gate G3 – Recommendation Freeze**

- **Approvers:** Purchase, ER, Quality, Finance and Program Manager  
- **Output:** Final techno-commercial evaluation, selected configuration, agreed modular price book, total business case, residual risks, and nomination recommendation.

### Step 6 — Supplier Nomination and Baseline Lock

Purchase compiles the digital nomination dossier automatically from the approved sourcing case. It includes the complete communication trail, TRSO versions, quotations, scorecards, audit findings, negotiation history, approval evidence, modular price book, capacity plan, localization roadmap, and risk actions.

**Gate G4 – Nomination Approval**

- **Mandatory signoffs:** Finance, Quality, ER, Program Manager and Purchase approving authority  
- **Additional signoff:** CPO/delegated authority where value, risk, single-source status, or policy threshold requires it  
- **Output:** Digitally signed nomination letter, locked baseline configuration and supplier acknowledgment.

---

## 4. Post-Nomination Design-Change Workflow

ER or the Program Manager initiates a **Change Request (CR)** against the nominated baseline. The request must identify the reason, affected TRSO requirements, variants, implementation date, expected volume, timing need, and preliminary technical classification.

The system automatically compares the proposed configuration with the nominated baseline and identifies affected modules. ER, Quality, Purchase, Supplier, Finance, and Program Management then perform a parallel impact assessment.

### 4.1 Change Classification and Routing

| Change route | Criteria | Approval and treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Route A — Pre-priced configuration change** | Uses an approved module; no new supplier/process; capacity, validation, tooling and price formula remain within the approved envelope | ER confirms applicability; Purchase validates calculated price; Program Manager confirms timing. Quality and Finance receive visibility and approve only if a flagged threshold is triggered. Target decision: **3 working days** |
| **Route B — Controlled deviation** | New or modified module, tooling, validation, material, capacity, or cost impact, but incumbent remains technically and commercially viable | Supplier submits delta quotation only. ER, Quality, Purchase, Finance and Program Manager approve affected elements. Unaffected baseline terms remain locked. Target decision: **7 working days** |
| **Route C — Fundamental change / re-source** | Major architecture or styling redesign; regulatory or safety impact; new technology beyond supplier capability; significant capacity/timing risk; or cost exceeds authority threshold | Reopen relevant sourcing stages, benchmark alternative suppliers, and obtain G2–G4 approvals as applicable. CPO/delegated authority approval required |

Thresholds for value, tooling, timing, capacity, and safety impact shall be configurable by commodity, program, and delegation-of-authority policy rather than hard-coded.

### 4.2 Change Approval Gate

**Gate G5 – Change Implementation Approval**

Required evidence includes:

- Revised TRSO/drawing and redline comparison;
- Affected module list and delta BOM;
- Supplier delta quotation and cost-driver evidence;
- Tooling, capacity, validation, quality and launch impact;
- Program timing and inventory/obsolescence impact;
- Updated business case and implementation date;
- Functional approvals appropriate to Route A, B, or C.

Following approval, the platform creates a new immutable baseline version, updates the nomination/contract record, and retains the complete link to all superseded versions. Rejected or withdrawn changes remain auditable.

---

## 5. Digital Platform—First-Level Functional Blueprint

TechSol should design the platform as a configurable workflow and product-configuration solution integrated with existing enterprise systems.

### Core Capabilities

1. **Structured master data:** Programs, lamp families, variants, suppliers, TRSO requirements, BOMs, modules, cost drivers, price indices and authority matrices.
2. **Workflow orchestration:** Configurable gates, parallel approvals, delegation, reminders, SLA timers, escalation and exception routing.
3. **Document and version control:** Controlled templates, redline comparison, digital signatures, check-in/check-out and immutable audit logs.
4. **Supplier portal:** Secure RFQ receipt, structured quotation submission, clarification management, revision history and acknowledgment.
5. **Quotation configurator:** Baseline-plus-module pricing, add/delete/replace simulation, should-cost comparison, scenario analysis and delta-quote generation.
6. **Evaluation workspace:** Weighted scorecards, side-by-side comparisons, risk register, deviation tracking and recommendation generation.
7. **Change-impact engine:** Baseline comparison, affected-module identification, threshold rules and automated Route A/B/C assignment.
8. **Dashboards:** Program milestone risk, pending approvals, aging, sourcing cycle time, change cycle time, supplier performance, savings/cost avoidance, and localization.
9. **Integration:** Product lifecycle management for TRSO/drawings/BOM; ERP for supplier, PO and price data; quality systems for audits and claims; finance systems for budgets and indices; identity services for access and signatures.
10. **Controls:** Role-based access, segregation of duties, encryption, retention policy, backup, disaster recovery, electronic signature compliance, exportable audit package and API-based architecture.

### Minimum Status Model

**Draft → Under Review → Approved for RFQ → RFQ Active → Evaluation → Negotiation → Recommendation → Approval → Nominated → Change Under Review → Revised Baseline → Closed/Cancelled**

Every transition must record the actor, date/time, comments, attachments, previous value, new value, and approval basis.

---

## 6. Governance and Success Measures

Purchase remains the process owner and custodian of the nomination record. ER owns technical requirements and revisions; Quality owns quality-risk acceptance; Finance owns financial validation; Program Management owns milestone and program-impact concurrence; TechSol owns platform design, availability, security, integration, and support.

The implementation should be piloted on one headlamp and one tail-lamp program before commodity-wide rollout.

**Recommended KPIs**

- Sourcing request-to-nomination lead time;
- Post-nomination change approval lead time by route;
- Percentage of changes processed through pre-priced modules;
- First-time-right TRSO and quotation completeness;
- Approval aging and SLA adherence by function;
- Cost variance versus nominated baseline;
- Number of full renegotiations avoided;
- Localization achievement, launch adherence, and supplier quality performance;
- Percentage of sourcing cases with a complete, audit-ready digital record.

This workflow preserves formal governance while shifting lamp sourcing from repeated document rework to controlled configuration management, enabling faster design evolution with full commercial and technical traceability.

## Sheet 3 — Lead Qualification Scorecard

Use this scorecard during and immediately after each meeting.

| Criterion | Weight | 1 — Low | 3 — Medium | 5 — High |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| **Platform relevance** | 20% | No underwater platform; only indirect interest | Integrates third-party submerged hardware | Manufactures AUV, ROV, robot, or underwater camera |
| **Aquaculture focus** | 15% | No active aquaculture activity | Occasional projects or distributor-led sales | Aquaculture is a core market |
| **DO customer value** | 15% | No clear use case | Useful as optional contextual data | DO solves a stated customer problem or closes a portfolio gap |
| **Technical integration readiness** | 15% | No spare power/data or closed architecture | Possible with engineering effort | Modular payload port, standard protocol, software support |
| **Deployment suitability** | 10% | Flow, depth, fouling, or service conditions unsuitable | Manageable with mechanical changes | Suitable flow and routine access for cleaning/calibration |
| **OEM volume potential** | 10% | One-off project | Tens of units or retrofit opportunity | Repeat production and meaningful installed base |
| **Decision-maker access** | 5% | General booth contact only | Referral promised | Product/engineering owner engaged |
| **Commercial timing** | 5% | More than 24 months or undefined | 12–24 months | Active 2025–2026 project |
| **Strategic leverage** | 5% | Isolated niche opportunity | Regional or segment influence | Major brand, channel, or platform ecosystem |

### Scoring formula

\[
\text{Weighted Lead Score} = \sum \left(\frac{\text{Criterion Score}}{5} \times \text{Weight}\right)
\]

| Weighted score | Disposition |
|---:|---|
| **80–100** | Immediate engineering and commercial follow-up |
| **65–79** | Qualified opportunity; schedule technical discovery |
| **50–64** | Nurture; resolve missing technical or commercial information |
| **Below 50** | Deprioritize unless strategic |
